sections.Astrophysical Alerts:
#### EP261111a gains a refined X-ray position and a tentative optical counterpart

Analysis reported on **12 November 2026 at 09:58:53 UTC** places the start of EP261111a at **11 November, 13:24:09 UTC**, 61 s before the WXT trigger. WXT followed the flare for approximately 60 s before the autonomous slew interrupted its light curve; this is not a measured full duration. The average unabsorbed **0.5–4 keV flux was \(1.30^{+0.65}_{-0.43}\times10^{-9}\) erg cm⁻² s⁻¹**, with photon index \(1.23^{+0.67}_{-0.64}\). FXT began at **13:28:25 UTC**, 256 s after the refined onset, and localized an uncatalogued source to **RA 43.1193°, Dec +44.4351°, with a 10-arcsec 90% confidence radius** including statistical and systematic errors. Its 3150-s observation gave average unabsorbed **0.5–10 keV flux \(3.15^{+0.41}_{-0.36}\times10^{-12}\) erg cm⁻² s⁻¹** and photon index \(1.90^{+0.15}_{-0.14}\). Spectral uncertainties are 90% intervals, with Galactic absorption fixed at \(N_H=1.10\times10^{21}\) cm⁻². The different energy bands and time averaging preclude interpreting the flux ratio as a precise decay factor. [GCN 46235](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46235).

An optical candidate was reported at **23:41:17 UTC on 12 November** from images obtained on **11 November**. Abastumani observations beginning **17:06:33 UTC** yield **R = 22.0 ± 0.3 Vega** at a midpoint 4.3 h after trigger, at **RA 02:52:28.0, Dec +44:26:05.3**, inside the refined FXT region. Mondy observations beginning **20:30:41 UTC** give **R > 22.5 at 3σ** at 7.6 h. The near-limit detection and subsequent upper limit support a fading-source candidate, but do not yet establish the association. [GCN 46242](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46242).

LCO imaging on **12 November**, beginning **01:59:08 and 08:12:07 UTC**, gives **r > 22.7 and z > 22.3 AB at 3σ**, respectively. Earlier SYSU observations on **11 November** give **K > 17.83 and J > 19.83 Vega at 5σ**, over 15:02:09–15:41:58 and 16:40:41–17:41:30 UTC. These limits do not exclude the faint optical candidate; filter differences, AB/Vega systems and uncorrected Galactic extinction prevent a direct color or decay fit. No redshift or physical classification is established by these reports. [GCN 46236](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46236), [GCN 46237](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46237).

#### An underlying Euclid source complicates the host assignment for EP261105a

A report issued on **12 November 2026 at 23:00:40 UTC** identifies a pre-existing, nearly point-like source in Euclid DR1 VIS imaging at the candidate optical counterpart of **EP261105a**, with **\(m_{\rm VIS}=24.93\pm0.06\)** (MAG_AUTO). The reported transient position is offset by approximately **0.15 arcsec**. Some surrounding extended emission is visible, but the imaging cannot distinguish a Galactic object, a compact object associated with the previously proposed **z = 0.0765** galaxy, or a more distant source. The circular does not specify the archival exposure date. [GCN 46241](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46241).

Assuming the faint object is a higher-redshift galaxy, a **0.1-arcsec half-light radius** and an association radius twice that value give the authors' chance-alignment estimate of **approximately 0.12%**. This conditional calculation is not a posterior host probability and does not supply a redshift. The new imaging therefore strengthens the need to resolve the underlying object's nature before using the nearby galaxy's distance to infer a kilonova-like luminosity. It does not establish a kilonova or disprove the alternative host. [GCN 46241](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46241), [host spectroscopy: GCN 46231](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46231).

#### GRB 261110A: refined prompt emission confirms a long, soft burst

SVOM/ECLAIRs analysis reported on **12 November 2026 at 08:18:22 UTC** characterizes the burst that triggered at **10 November, 11:50:00 UTC** as a single broad pulse with **\(T_{90}=32^{+8}_{-5}\) s in 4–120 keV**. The spectrum accumulated from **31.84 to 0.32 s before the onboard trigger** is fitted over 5–120 keV by a power law with index **\(\alpha=-2.01\pm0.20\)**. The model gives **4–120 keV fluence \((2.36\pm0.48)\times10^{-7}\) erg cm⁻²** and photon flux **\(0.301\pm0.061\) photons cm⁻² s⁻¹**; all quoted errors are **68% confidence**. These are prompt-emission measurements complementing the previously reported fading optical afterglow. The circular does not determine a spectral peak or an isotropic-equivalent energy. [GCN 46234](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46234).

#### GRB 261026A remains optically detectable more than fifteen days after the burst

CrAO/ZTSh observations obtained on **10 November 2026 from 16:05:36 to 17:35:39 UTC**, and reported on **12 November at 17:26:34 UTC**, detect the established optical counterpart of GRB 261026A at **R = 23.28 ± 0.25 Vega**, at a midpoint **15.44515 days after the burst**. The stacked exposure was **43 × 120 s**, with a **3σ limiting magnitude R = 24.6**. This extends the measured optical emission into the late-time regime; the single new point alone does not distinguish an afterglow component from any underlying host or supernova contribution. The preliminary photometry is not corrected for Galactic extinction. [GCN 46240](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46240).

#### EP-WXT trigger 01709322455 is probably a flare from G 6-43

The EP team classified the trigger at **12 November 2026, 13:22:27 UTC** as a likely stellar flare associated with **G 6-43**, reporting at **14:30:37 UTC** an estimated **0.5–4 keV flux ≈ 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁰ erg cm⁻² s⁻¹** and corresponding luminosity **≈ 3.2 × 10³¹ erg s⁻¹**. No uncertainties or association probability were supplied. [GCN 46238](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46238).

SVOM/C-GFT reported on **13 November at 06:59:31 UTC** that G 6-43 faded in g, r and i over approximately 1.98 h, with the largest amplitude in g, consistent with stellar-flare decay. The circular's **body identifies trigger 01709322455 and G 6-43, but its subject line names the older trigger 01709322272**; its stated start time and relative delay are also inconsistent. The optical evidence is therefore linked here by the explicit source identification, without adopting the ambiguous timing. This is a likely stellar classification, not a confirmed extragalactic transient. [GCN 46243](https://gcn.nasa.gov/circulars/46243).
